content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies algorithmic fairness. The authors propose adversarial training for representation debiasing. Experiments on tabular, graph, and image data show the proposed technique gained improvements in terms of both accuracy and fairness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:

1.  The authors conduct comprehensive experiments on different types of data including tabular, images, and graphs.

2. The attribution explanation is interesting and looks easy to apply.

Cons:

1. The introductory part is too long and somehow redundant. Instead of reviewing all relevant papers in fairness and multiple applications, I would like to see the unifying idea of this paper: the motivation, and the high-level idea of the proposed solution. Reviewing such a significant amount of literature does not help readers get into your contributions. The authors offer limited explanations of what they did in the abstract and introduction but only some meaningless words like 'powerful strategy' and 'effective.'

2. The paper contains limited novelty and insight. The only difference I can see compared to adversarial debiasing [1] is the authors train different parts of a neural network with different objective functions Eq. (2) and (3). However, the authors fail to convince me why we should do that and why it works. Prop. 2.1 looks intuitive to me but does not answer my concern.

3. Adversarial training may bring some instability to the final results. However, the authors do not report standard deviation to reveal the real performance.

[1] Mitigating Unwanted Biases with Adversarial Learning, AIES'18

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper targets the problem of group fairness w.r.t to a set of protected attributes. The setting is binary classification problems on tabular, graph, and image data, though the proposed method is general and applicable to multi-class classification problems. The proposed method involves training a module parallel to the backbone model that maximizes fairness. The complete approach can be formulated as a minimax game, and yields favorable experimental results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper targets an important area (fairness), the method is simple (in the sense of having few components) and has a clear motivation. The method is model agnostic and is not limited to any specific domain.

Unfortunately, the paper has some flaws. 

1. Inadequately positioned with respect to prior work. The idea of framing fairness as an adversarial game is not new, but the authors do not clarify the differences between their work and the existing body of literature. For example, what are the differences between this work and [1,2]? Both employ the same basic technique, and are several years old at this point. 

2. Poor quality figures. The main architecture diagram (Fig. 1) is not comprehensible and I do not understand it, in addition to being in a different font and font size from the main paper. Fig 2,3,4 are unreadable, with the text being literally pixels large on my screen after zooming. Because the main results for the vision section are entirely in a figure, I cannot verify if the author's claims are correct. 

3. Does Table 1 show demographic parity or accuracy? There are two datasets, each with one column dedicated to it. The caption does not match the table. 

4. The authors claim to compare to state of the art baselines, but in the Graph section (3.2) all the baselines are from before 2020, and in the image section, there is only one baseline within the past two years (FairMixup, 2021). 

Regarding FairMixup, this sentence:
> "Over 200,000 celebrity photos of faces can be found in CelebA, where each image is assigned 40 human-labeled binary characteristics, including gender. We choose attractive, smiling, and wavy hair among the attributes and utilize them in three binary classification tasks, considering gender as the protected attribute. We chose these three characteristics because each of these activities has a sensitive group that receives a disproportionately high number of positive samples."

reads almost like a copypasta of the sentence from the FairMixup paper:

> "CelebA contains over 200,000 images of celebrity faces, where each image is associated with 40 human-labeled binary attributes including gender. Among the attributes, we select attractive, smile, and wavy hair and use them to form three binary classification tasks while treating gender as the sensitive attribute. The reason we choose these three attributes is that there exists in all these tasks, a sensitive group that has more positive samples than the other one".


References:
[1] Adel, Tameem et al. “One-Network Adversarial Fairness.” AAAI (2019).
[2] Wadsworth, Christina et al. “Achieving Fairness through Adversarial Learning: an Application to Recidivism Prediction.” ArXiv abs/1807.00199 (2018)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
It is difficult to assess the novelty of the work because the authors do not adequately position their work relative to the literature. IMO, the proposed method appears to be straightforward adversarial training (using a single network instead of an adversary network), which has already been proposed, for example by [1,2]. Note: These are just two papers I searched, there may be many more which employ a similar method. The authors should clearly set off differences between their paper and prior work. 

The clarity of the paper needs to be greatly improved. The biggest issue is the low quality figures containing critical results. The other issue is the writing, it is very informal and imprecise in parts. For example

>This section introduces a new approach for training a fair classifier based on deep neural networks. The *proposed deep learning
model includes two sets of weights for a classifier neural network*. This model can consist of different neural network layers (FF, GCN, CNN, ...). The first set of weights is related to the classification task of the DL model, and the second is related to the Distraction module, which is *the fairness part of the model*.

The paper does not introduce a new model, (or even new module, MLP is not novel) but a new training procedure. Saying things like "this is the fairness part of the model" is also jarring to read in a scientific publication. 




References:
[1] Adel, Tameem et al. “One-Network Adversarial Fairness.” AAAI (2019).
[2] Wadsworth, Christina et al. “Achieving Fairness through Adversarial Learning: an Application to Recidivism Prediction.” ArXiv abs/1807.00199 (2018)
content.summary_of_the_review: The experimental results of the paper are strong relative to the baselines compared against. However, many of the baselines are very old by now (see the strengths and weaknesses section), and several of the results are in unreadable figures making it difficult to analyze the claims of the authors. The central claims of the paper are written in imprecise language (authors say they introduce a new model, and sometimes a new module, but what they really mean is they introduce a new training procedure), and given that the new training procedure seems to be very similar to single-network adversarial training, the novelty of the paper is unclear.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a "distraction module" which constitutes a set of hidden layers that optimize for a group fairness loss whereas the (entire) original network aims to optimize for the original classification task. In this way, the DNN can learn to output classifications that are invariant to the protected groups/sensitive attributes. The authors study their approach through empirical experiments on 3 categories of datasets: "tabular", "graph-based", and "vision-based".
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper proposes a new approach which modifies the original architecture provided for a deep learning based classification task by adding a "distraction" module.
- The authors conduct experiments on three different dataset domains, from tabular, to graph- and vision-based.

Weaknesses:
- Technical Issues: 
My main concern with the paper is regarding the approach itself-- I am not fully convinced that the distraction module's addition to the original network architecture trivially leads to favorably fair and accurate classifications. I have outlined my major concerns regarding the approach along three dimensions below, and I hope the authors can provide more evidence to counter these concerns:
1. Theoretical Convergence: I am not sure that the proposed optimization approach results in convergence to favorable solutions. I believe the proof provided in Proposition 2.1 is somewhat circular, since $\theta_c$ is kept fixed and assumed to be optimal. Firstly, this assumption should be provided in the theorem statement. Secondly, under this assumption quite evidently the other loss will converge to a solution that is independent of the protected groups; however if we are iteratively optimizing both modules, how is this guaranteed? A simple analogy can be made to the first versions of Generative Adversarial Networks, who have a similar minimax formulation but there is no guarantee that they will converge to the Nash Equilibrium of the minimax game since Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) was not designed for this. The entire "proof" hinges on this assumption of optimality so I would like the authors to provide a stronger proof of the claim they seek to make. Note that the proposition statement is also circular: "the optimal $C(x, D(x))$ is an optimal classifier..". Further, the authors mention in the proof that $D(x)$ is updated with "sufficiently small steps" and "sufficiently small changes in $\theta_d$". Can these steps/changes be quantified? 
2. Empirical Convergence: Throughout the paper there is no mention of whether this approach converges empirically especially since it constitutes an architecture change. For example, training loss curves should be presented with respect to both individual losses over iterations. Further, does introducing the distraction module add issues with training and convergence? Are the layers overfitting to the input data? These are some of the experiments I would like to see, which are currently missing from the paper.
3. Lack of Experimental Evidence: The authors conduct limited experiments to fully analyze the claims made in the paper. (a) For example, for vision, only the CelebA dataset is considered. It would be beneficial to see results on other high-dimensional vision datasets, especially with more protected attributes other than gender. (b) Furthermore, while the authors state that they only focus on binary classification without loss of generality, I believe this is not sufficient. It would be beneficial to see results for >2 class classification and then observe the empirical convergence results. I feel that multi-class classification might even lead to convergence issues. (c) Further, how are the competitive methods chosen? For all dataset categories a large majority of the methods being compared with are from before 2020. The authors should compare more with recent work, such as [1] for the tabular dataset scenario. Comparisons with more recent SOTA methods will help gauge the novelty of the approach.

- Formatting and Presentation Issues:
The paper has numerous typos and presentation/consistency issues that should be corrected. (a) For example, why aren't all the figures /metrics' tables consistent across all three dataset categories? I believe statistical parity can be plotted with accuracy for all classification tasks with similar formatting to aid readability, and parity-accuracy curve area values can be provided for all categories. If there is a justifiable reason for presenting results the way it has been done in the paper, the authors should make the reasons for this clear in the beginning of the results section. (b) Next, equations are often referred to without using Eq. before the number so this also hinders readability. (c) The authors should use \citep{} to reference most of the papers in the text, as most references that should have parentheses are missing them at the moment. (d) Please make the notation consistent-- for example, ($C, C(x, D(x)),$C), are all used interchangeably for the entire network and ($D(x),$D) are both used to refer to the Discriminator module.

- References:
[1] https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2021/file/44e207aecc63505eb828d442de03f2e9-Paper.pdf
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Clarity and Quality: Please refer to "Formatting and Presentation Issues" under "Weaknesses" above.
- Novelty: Please refer to additional experiments under "Lack of Experimental Evidence" under "Teachnical Issues" ("Weaknesses") above.
- Reproducibility: The authors have provided source code for experiments but I have not reproduced results myself.
content.summary_of_the_review: I am recommending the paper for rejection pending additional experiments and theoretical results to justify the claims made. My review encompasses the technical issues, related to analytical claims, convergence, and lack of in-depth experimentation. I have also highlighted several areas in which presentation is lacking and can be improved upon.
